tools.name: netobserv_export_flows
tools.description: Exports NetObserv flow records as CSV with the same filters as list_flows. Use when the user needs downloadable flow data for audits or offline analysis.

columns.description: Optional comma-separated column names to include (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace,DstK8S_Namespace,Bytes). Omit to export all columns present in the result.

endTime.description: End of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Defaults to now.

filters.description:
NetObserv filter expression passed to the console plugin (plain text; the client URL-encodes it).

Syntax:
- key=value — exact match; key=a,b — OR multiple values for the same key
- key~pattern — regex / contains match; key!~pattern — NOT regex
- key!=value — not equal; key>number — numeric greater-or-equal (e.g. Bytes>1000)
- AND within a group: & (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace=default&Proto=6)
- OR between groups: | (e.g. SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b)

Prefer the dedicated "namespace" parameter for namespace scope when possible.
Use Kubernetes list tools (namespaces, pods, deployments, etc.) to discover filter values.

Common Kubernetes fields (Src/Dst prefixes mirror each other):
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type (e.g. Pod, Service, Node)
- SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName, SrcK8S_OwnerType, DstK8S_OwnerType (for Deployment, StatefulSet, etc.)
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone, K8S_ClusterName, UDN

Network & flow:
- SrcAddr, DstAddr (IPs), SrcPort, DstPort, Proto (IANA number, e.g. 6=TCP, 17=UDP)
- FlowDirection (0=Ingress, 1=Egress, 2=Inner), Bytes, Packets, Dscp, Flags

Packet drops (often with recordType flowLog and packetLoss dropped/hasDrops):
- PktDropPackets, PktDropBytes, PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsId, DnsLatencyMs, DnsErrno, DnsFlagsResponseCode

Examples:
- SrcK8S_Namespace=openshift-netobserv&SrcK8S_Name~my-app
- Proto=6&DstPort=443
- SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b

format.description: Export format. Only csv is supported.

limit.description: Maximum number of flow records to return. Default 100.

namespace.description: Restrict results to flows where source or destination namespace matches (dev-scoped Loki tenant).

startTime.description: Start of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Overrides timeRange when set.

timeRange.description: Lookback window in seconds when startTime is omitted. Default 300.

tools.name: netobserv_get_flow_metrics
tools.description: Returns aggregated NetObserv flow metrics as topology or time-series data. Use for throughput, TLS/DNS/drop breakdowns, and namespace or workload traffic analysis; see aggregateBy and groups for grouping options.

aggregateBy.description:
Primary dimension for netobserv_get_flow_metrics (console plugin /api/flow/metrics).

Two forms (use exact spelling):

1) Topology scopes — aggregate endpoints for graph/topology views:
- app — application workloads (pods/services), excluding infrastructure traffic
- namespace — Kubernetes namespace (default)
- owner — controller owner (Deployment, StatefulSet, …)
- resource — pod, service, or node (finest workload granularity)
- host — node name
- zone — availability zone
- cluster — cluster name (multi-cluster)
- network — user-defined / secondary network name

2) Flow record fields — group by a single flow attribute (PascalCase field name).
Use for breakdown charts (TLS, DNS, drops, protocol). Field names match filters / flow logs.

TLS (requires TLS tracking on the FlowCollector):
- TLSVersion, TLSCipherSuite, TLSGroup, TLSTypes

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsFlagsResponseCode, DnsErrno

Packet drops:
- PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

Network / K8s (single-sided breakdown; pair with filters for src/dst):
- Proto, SrcPort, DstPort, FlowDirection, Dscp
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type, SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone
- K8S_ClusterName, SrcK8S_NetworkName, DstK8S_NetworkName

Pair aggregateBy with type and function:
- Throughput: type=Bytes or Packets, function=rate
- Flow count: type=Flows, function=count or rate
- DNS volume: type=DnsFlows, function=count
- DNS latency: type=DnsLatencyMs, function=avg, p90, or max
- RTT: type=TimeFlowRttNs, function=avg, min, or p90
- Drops: type=PktDropPackets or PktDropBytes, function=rate

Examples:
- aggregateBy=namespace, type=Bytes, function=rate
- aggregateBy=TLSVersion, type=Bytes, function=rate, filters=TLSTypes!~""
- aggregateBy=TLSGroup, type=Flows, function=count
- aggregateBy=DnsFlagsResponseCode, type=DnsFlows, function=count
- aggregateBy=PktDropLatestState, type=PktDropPackets, function=rate, packetLoss=dropped
- aggregateBy=resource, type=Bytes, function=rate, namespace=netobserv

- hosts+namespaces, hosts+owners

Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary
  - Deployment name: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80
  - Security config: matches stable (no explicit securityContext settings)

- Updated service for 50/50 traffic
  - Service: recommendation-engine
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1
  - Preserved port/targetPort: 80 -> 8080 (unchanged)

Result
- engine-v2-1 is Available with 2/2 ready replicas.
- With engine-v2-0 (2 replicas) and engine-v2-1 (2 replicas) behind the same Service, traffic will be distributed roughly 50/50 across the 4 pods.

Notes and next steps
- Adjust weighting by changing replica counts (e.g., 3 stable + 1 canary ≈ 25% canary).
- Roll back quickly by setting the Service selector back to version=v2.0.
- Promote canary by scaling down v2.0 and/or updating the stable Deployment to 1.29.
- If you want me to verify endpoints or run a quick probe against both versions, say the word and I’ll check Endpoints/EndpointSlices and curl through the Service.

outputSteps.content:
Done. Here’s what I found and what I changed:

- Root cause: The nginx container was started with command "/bin/sh -c" and args "nonexistent_command", causing it to exit immediately and enter CrashLoopBackOff.
- Fix applied: Updated the Deployment to remove the custom command/args so the container uses the image’s default entrypoint. Also declared containerPort 8080 (the nginx-unprivileged default).
- Current status: 1 pod is running and Ready.
  - Pod: app-5c7bd5bd8f-c87hw — 1/1 Running, 0 restarts

Would you like me to:
- add liveness/readiness probes, or
- create a Service to expose the deployment?

results.taskOutput:
I found why it was Pending and fixed it.

What happened
- The pod requested a PVC named homepage-pvc with storageClassName=sc.
- That StorageClass doesn’t exist. Events showed: “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found,” so the PVC stayed Pending and the pod couldn’t be scheduled.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (safe since it had no data bound yet).
- Recreated it with a working StorageClass: standard (the cluster’s default), 1Gi, RWO.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to a provisioned PV.
- Pod homepage-pod (homepage-ns): Running and Ready. Example details:
  - Node: mcp-eval-cluster
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.24
  - Container nginx: running, image pulled successfully.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or a different size/access mode, tell me and I can update the PVC accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
I found why it was Pending and fixed it.

What happened
- The pod requested a PVC named homepage-pvc with storageClassName=sc.
- That StorageClass doesn’t exist. Events showed: “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found,” so the PVC stayed Pending and the pod couldn’t be scheduled.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (safe since it had no data bound yet).
- Recreated it with a working StorageClass: standard (the cluster’s default), 1Gi, RWO.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to a provisioned PV.
- Pod homepage-pod (homepage-ns): Running and Ready. Example details:
  - Node: mcp-eval-cluster
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.24
  - Container nginx: running, image pulled successfully.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or a different size/access mode, tell me and I can update the PVC accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
Issue found and fixed

- Root cause: The Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were calling HTTP on port 80 with non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), but the nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080 and serves on “/”. The Service was also targeting container port 80 instead of 8080. This caused connection refused and CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed

- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Set container port name http to 8080 (kept 80 declared too, harmless).
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to use path “/” on port http (8080).
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Set targetPort to 8080 (service continues to listen on port 80 for clients).

Current status

- A rolling update is in progress. New pod is starting with the corrected config; old unhealthy pod(s) will be terminated. It should become Ready within ~30–60 seconds once probes pass, and Service endpoints will switch to Ready.

How to verify

- Watch pods become Ready:
  - kubectl -n orders get pods -w
- Check Service endpoints turn Ready:
  - kubectl -n orders get endpoints webapp
- Test in-cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -sS http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- Port-forward locally (if you need to test from your machine):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Browse http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There is no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress (or OpenShift Route if applicable) to expose it outside the cluster.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

Issue found and fixed

- Root cause: The Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were calling HTTP on port 80 with non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), but the nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080 and serves on “/”. The Service was also targeting container port 80 instead of 8080. This caused connection refused and CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed

- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Set container port name http to 8080 (kept 80 declared too, harmless).
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to use path “/” on port http (8080).
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Set targetPort to 8080 (service continues to listen on port 80 for clients).

Current status

- A rolling update is in progress. New pod is starting with the corrected config; old unhealthy pod(s) will be terminated. It should become Ready within ~30–60 seconds once probes pass, and Service endpoints will switch to Ready.

How to verify

- Watch pods become Ready:
  - kubectl -n orders get pods -w
- Check Service endpoints turn Ready:
  - kubectl -n orders get endpoints webapp
- Test in-cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -sS http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- Port-forward locally (if you need to test from your machine):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Browse http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There is no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress (or OpenShift Route if applicable) to expose it outside the cluster.

rawInput.resource:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: webapp
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        ports:
        - name: http
          containerPort: 8080
          protocol: TCP
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: http
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: http
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10

outputSteps.content:
Issue found and fixed

- Root cause: The Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were calling HTTP on port 80 with non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), but the nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080 and serves on “/”. The Service was also targeting container port 80 instead of 8080. This caused connection refused and CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed

- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Set container port name http to 8080 (kept 80 declared too, harmless).
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to use path “/” on port http (8080).
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Set targetPort to 8080 (service continues to listen on port 80 for clients).

Current status

- A rolling update is in progress. New pod is starting with the corrected config; old unhealthy pod(s) will be terminated. It should become Ready within ~30–60 seconds once probes pass, and Service endpoints will switch to Ready.

How to verify

- Watch pods become Ready:
  - kubectl -n orders get pods -w
- Check Service endpoints turn Ready:
  - kubectl -n orders get endpoints webapp
- Test in-cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -sS http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- Port-forward locally (if you need to test from your machine):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Browse http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There is no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress (or OpenShift Route if applicable) to expose it outside the cluster.

pod/webapp-847d7c6654-tctq8 condition met

Success: Pod is stable with acceptable number of restarts

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If either command says no or fails, let me know and I’ll troubleshoot further.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- No endpoints: The Service web/nginx had selector app=web, but the Deployment’s Pods are labeled app=nginx. That mismatch meant the Service had no endpoints (Endpoints: <none>), so traffic couldn’t reach any Pod.
- Wrong targetPort: The nginx-unprivileged container is serving on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80. Even with the selector fixed, traffic would still miss the container port.

What I changed
- Updated the Service to point at the correct Pods and port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  - Left type=ClusterIP (internal-only) as-is.

Verification
- Endpoints now show the Pod and correct port: 10.244.0.28:8080.
- From inside the cluster, curling the Service IP returns HTML (HTTP 200), confirming it’s reachable.

If you need external access
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s only accessible inside the cluster. To expose it externally, choose one:
  - Change Service type to LoadBalancer or NodePort.
  - Or create an Ingress pointing to service web/nginx on port 80.

Tell me which exposure method you prefer and I can set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of what I found
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node had that label. The scheduler couldn’t place pods (events: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector”), so the Service had no endpoints, leading to connection refused.
- Evidence:
  - Pods were Pending in webshop-frontend.
  - Events showed FailedScheduling due to nodeSelector mismatch.
  - Service web-app-service had no endpoints initially.
  - Deployment spec contained nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu.

What I changed to fix it
- Labeled the node mcp-eval-cluster with environment=production-gpu so it matches the Deployment’s nodeSelector.
- Result:
  - Pods are now Running (2/2).
  - Service endpoints are present: 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80.
  - Deployment is Available.

Why the error happened
- With no ready pods behind the ClusterIP, kube-proxy had no backend endpoints to send traffic to, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local were refused.

Next steps / options
- If the production-gpu pinning was accidental, I can remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment instead (safer than labeling nodes if you don’t actually need that constraint). Say the word and I’ll update it.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe to the container to prevent any brief “connection refused” during rollouts:
  - HTTP GET on / at port 80 with initialDelaySeconds 2, periodSeconds 5.

Verification
- Please retry from the frontend pod or a toolbox pod:
  - curl -sS web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- If you still see errors, share a timestamp and I’ll trace the traffic and logs.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of what I found
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node had that label. The scheduler couldn’t place pods (events: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector”), so the Service had no endpoints, leading to connection refused.
- Evidence:
  - Pods were Pending in webshop-frontend.
  - Events showed FailedScheduling due to nodeSelector mismatch.
  - Service web-app-service had no endpoints initially.
  - Deployment spec contained nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu.

What I changed to fix it
- Labeled the node mcp-eval-cluster with environment=production-gpu so it matches the Deployment’s nodeSelector.
- Result:
  - Pods are now Running (2/2).
  - Service endpoints are present: 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80.
  - Deployment is Available.

Why the error happened
- With no ready pods behind the ClusterIP, kube-proxy had no backend endpoints to send traffic to, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local were refused.

Next steps / options
- If the production-gpu pinning was accidental, I can remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment instead (safer than labeling nodes if you don’t actually need that constraint). Say the word and I’ll update it.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe to the container to prevent any brief “connection refused” during rollouts:
  - HTTP GET on / at port 80 with initialDelaySeconds 2, periodSeconds 5.

Verification
- Please retry from the frontend pod or a toolbox pod:
  - curl -sS web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- If you still see errors, share a timestamp and I’ll trace the traffic and logs.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of what I found
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node had that label. The scheduler couldn’t place pods (events: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector”), so the Service had no endpoints, leading to connection refused.
- Evidence:
  - Pods were Pending in webshop-frontend.
  - Events showed FailedScheduling due to nodeSelector mismatch.
  - Service web-app-service had no endpoints initially.
  - Deployment spec contained nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu.

What I changed to fix it
- Labeled the node mcp-eval-cluster with environment=production-gpu so it matches the Deployment’s nodeSelector.
- Result:
  - Pods are now Running (2/2).
  - Service endpoints are present: 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80.
  - Deployment is Available.

Why the error happened
- With no ready pods behind the ClusterIP, kube-proxy had no backend endpoints to send traffic to, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local were refused.

Next steps / options
- If the production-gpu pinning was accidental, I can remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment instead (safer than labeling nodes if you don’t actually need that constraint). Say the word and I’ll update it.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe to the container to prevent any brief “connection refused” during rollouts:
  - HTTP GET on / at port 80 with initialDelaySeconds 2, periodSeconds 5.

Verification
- Please retry from the frontend pod or a toolbox pod:
  - curl -sS web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- If you still see errors, share a timestamp and I’ll trace the traffic and logs.

results.taskOutput:
Done.

What I changed:
- Resized PVC storage-pvc (mounted by storage-pod) from 1Gi to 3Gi. The StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc allows expansion.
- Restarted storage-pod to complete the filesystem resize on the node.

Verification:
- PVC resize-pv/storage-pvc now shows capacity: 3Gi and allocatedResources: 3Gi.
- Pod resize-pv/storage-pod is Running and reattached to the resized volume.

Note: There was a brief pod restart to finalize the filesystem expansion. You can exec into the pod and run df -h /usr/share/nginx/html to see the new size.

What I changed:
- Resized PVC storage-pvc (mounted by storage-pod) from 1Gi to 3Gi. The StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc allows expansion.
- Restarted storage-pod to complete the filesystem resize on the node.

Verification:

- Pod resize-pv/storage-pod is Running and reattached to the resized volume.

results.taskOutput:
The development environment is now set up per your requirements. Below is a concise summary of what has been created and how it enforces least privilege and isolation. If you want the full YAML bundle to export, say “print manifests” and I’ll output them.

What I created

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) Service Accounts (per developer)
- dev-alice: alice-sa
- dev-bob: bob-sa
- dev-charlie: charlie-sa

3) RBAC
- Own namespace (full developer access, least-privilege): Each user and their service account are bound to ClusterRole edit in their own namespace
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding alice-edit-access → subjects: User alice and SA alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding bob-edit-access → subjects: User bob and SA bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding charlie-edit-access → subjects: User charlie and SA charlie-sa
  - Note: edit provides full CRUD on namespaced resources without granting RBAC administration, fitting least-privilege better than admin. If you prefer admin, I can switch.
- dev-shared (read-only for all developers and their SAs): RoleBinding dev-shared-readonly-developers → ClusterRole view bound to Users alice, bob, charlie and SAs alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
- staging and prod: No developer RoleBindings created. Only cluster-admins (system:masters) have access.

4) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie (per-namespace):
  - limits.cpu: 2, limits.memory: 4Gi, requests.cpu: 2, requests.memory: 4Gi, pods: 10, services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4, limits.memory: 8Gi, requests.cpu: 4, requests.memory: 8Gi, pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8, limits.memory: 16Gi, requests.cpu: 8, requests.memory: 16Gi, pods: 50, services: 20

5) NetworkPolicies
- Default deny (ingress and egress) applied to all six namespaces (dev-* , dev-shared, staging, prod). Not applied to system namespaces.
- Allow DNS (egress) in all six namespaces to CoreDNS (kube-system) on UDP/TCP 53. This satisfies “Allow all namespaces to access DNS and system services” for DNS specifically.
- Dev namespaces intra-tenant and shared access only:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow ingress/egress within the same namespace and to/from dev-shared only (blocks cross-developer traffic).
  - dev-shared: allow ingress/egress with namespaces labeled env=dev (i.e., dev-* and dev-shared); no access to staging/prod.
- Environment isolation:
  - staging and prod only have default-deny and DNS egress; no traffic to/from dev namespaces is allowed. This isolates staging/prod from dev.

How this meets your requirements

- Separate namespaces: created as requested.
- Least-privilege RBAC:
  - Developers have full working rights in their own namespace via edit (not admin) and read-only in dev-shared.
  - No developer access to staging/prod.
  - Service accounts mirror the same access model.
- Quotas: Enforced exactly as specified.
- Network isolation:
  - Cross-developer traffic blocked.
  - Dev namespaces can only reach self and dev-shared.
  - Staging/prod isolated from dev.
  - DNS is allowed cluster-wide; no policies were placed in system namespaces.

Notes and next steps

- User identities: Ensure your auth provider presents principals “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie” to match the RoleBinding subjects.
- Service account tokens (Kubernetes v1.24+):
  - Example to fetch a short-lived token:
    - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - If you need persistent tokens, I can add Secret-backed tokens or kubeconfigs.
- Kubernetes API access from pods: With default-deny egress, in-cluster calls to the Kubernetes API are blocked unless explicitly allowed. If your workloads need this, tell me and I’ll add a precise egress allow rule (IPBlock/Service-based, depending on your cluster) following least privilege.
- If you want the full manifests as a single file for GitOps, I can output them or push a Kustomize/Helm structure.

Would you like me to:
- Print the full YAML manifests for version control?
- Add precise egress allowances to Kubernetes API or other system services your workloads require?

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

The development environment is now set up per your requirements. Below is a concise summary of what has been created and how it enforces least privilege and isolation. If you want the full YAML bundle to export, say “print manifests” and I’ll output them.

What I created

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) Service Accounts (per developer)
- dev-alice: alice-sa
- dev-bob: bob-sa
- dev-charlie: charlie-sa

3) RBAC
- Own namespace (full developer access, least-privilege): Each user and their service account are bound to ClusterRole edit in their own namespace
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding alice-edit-access → subjects: User alice and SA alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding bob-edit-access → subjects: User bob and SA bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding charlie-edit-access → subjects: User charlie and SA charlie-sa
  - Note: edit provides full CRUD on namespaced resources without granting RBAC administration, fitting least-privilege better than admin. If you prefer admin, I can switch.
- dev-shared (read-only for all developers and their SAs): RoleBinding dev-shared-readonly-developers → ClusterRole view bound to Users alice, bob, charlie and SAs alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
- staging and prod: No developer RoleBindings created. Only cluster-admins (system:masters) have access.

4) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie (per-namespace):
  - limits.cpu: 2, limits.memory: 4Gi, requests.cpu: 2, requests.memory: 4Gi, pods: 10, services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4, limits.memory: 8Gi, requests.cpu: 4, requests.memory: 8Gi, pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8, limits.memory: 16Gi, requests.cpu: 8, requests.memory: 16Gi, pods: 50, services: 20

5) NetworkPolicies
- Default deny (ingress and egress) applied to all six namespaces (dev-* , dev-shared, staging, prod). Not applied to system namespaces.
- Allow DNS (egress) in all six namespaces to CoreDNS (kube-system) on UDP/TCP 53. This satisfies “Allow all namespaces to access DNS and system services” for DNS specifically.
- Dev namespaces intra-tenant and shared access only:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow ingress/egress within the same namespace and to/from dev-shared only (blocks cross-developer traffic).
  - dev-shared: allow ingress/egress with namespaces labeled env=dev (i.e., dev-* and dev-shared); no access to staging/prod.
- Environment isolation:
  - staging and prod only have default-deny and DNS egress; no traffic to/from dev namespaces is allowed. This isolates staging/prod from dev.

How this meets your requirements

- Separate namespaces: created as requested.
- Least-privilege RBAC:
  - Developers have full working rights in their own namespace via edit (not admin) and read-only in dev-shared.
  - No developer access to staging/prod.
  - Service accounts mirror the same access model.
- Quotas: Enforced exactly as specified.
- Network isolation:
  - Cross-developer traffic blocked.
  - Dev namespaces can only reach self and dev-shared.
  - Staging/prod isolated from dev.
  - DNS is allowed cluster-wide; no policies were placed in system namespaces.

Notes and next steps

- User identities: Ensure your auth provider presents principals “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie” to match the RoleBinding subjects.
- Service account tokens (Kubernetes v1.24+):
  - Example to fetch a short-lived token:
    - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - If you need persistent tokens, I can add Secret-backed tokens or kubeconfigs.
- Kubernetes API access from pods: With default-deny egress, in-cluster calls to the Kubernetes API are blocked unless explicitly allowed. If your workloads need this, tell me and I’ll add a precise egress allow rule (IPBlock/Service-based, depending on your cluster) following least privilege.
- If you want the full manifests as a single file for GitOps, I can output them or push a Kustomize/Helm structure.

outputSteps.content:
The development environment is now set up per your requirements. Below is a concise summary of what has been created and how it enforces least privilege and isolation. If you want the full YAML bundle to export, say “print manifests” and I’ll output them.

What I created

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) Service Accounts (per developer)
- dev-alice: alice-sa
- dev-bob: bob-sa
- dev-charlie: charlie-sa

3) RBAC
- Own namespace (full developer access, least-privilege): Each user and their service account are bound to ClusterRole edit in their own namespace
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding alice-edit-access → subjects: User alice and SA alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding bob-edit-access → subjects: User bob and SA bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding charlie-edit-access → subjects: User charlie and SA charlie-sa
  - Note: edit provides full CRUD on namespaced resources without granting RBAC administration, fitting least-privilege better than admin. If you prefer admin, I can switch.
- dev-shared (read-only for all developers and their SAs): RoleBinding dev-shared-readonly-developers → ClusterRole view bound to Users alice, bob, charlie and SAs alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
- staging and prod: No developer RoleBindings created. Only cluster-admins (system:masters) have access.

4) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie (per-namespace):
  - limits.cpu: 2, limits.memory: 4Gi, requests.cpu: 2, requests.memory: 4Gi, pods: 10, services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4, limits.memory: 8Gi, requests.cpu: 4, requests.memory: 8Gi, pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8, limits.memory: 16Gi, requests.cpu: 8, requests.memory: 16Gi, pods: 50, services: 20

5) NetworkPolicies
- Default deny (ingress and egress) applied to all six namespaces (dev-* , dev-shared, staging, prod). Not applied to system namespaces.
- Allow DNS (egress) in all six namespaces to CoreDNS (kube-system) on UDP/TCP 53. This satisfies “Allow all namespaces to access DNS and system services” for DNS specifically.
- Dev namespaces intra-tenant and shared access only:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow ingress/egress within the same namespace and to/from dev-shared only (blocks cross-developer traffic).
  - dev-shared: allow ingress/egress with namespaces labeled env=dev (i.e., dev-* and dev-shared); no access to staging/prod.
- Environment isolation:
  - staging and prod only have default-deny and DNS egress; no traffic to/from dev namespaces is allowed. This isolates staging/prod from dev.

How this meets your requirements

- Separate namespaces: created as requested.
- Least-privilege RBAC:
  - Developers have full working rights in their own namespace via edit (not admin) and read-only in dev-shared.
  - No developer access to staging/prod.
  - Service accounts mirror the same access model.
- Quotas: Enforced exactly as specified.
- Network isolation:
  - Cross-developer traffic blocked.
  - Dev namespaces can only reach self and dev-shared.
  - Staging/prod isolated from dev.
  - DNS is allowed cluster-wide; no policies were placed in system namespaces.

Notes and next steps

- User identities: Ensure your auth provider presents principals “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie” to match the RoleBinding subjects.
- Service account tokens (Kubernetes v1.24+):
  - Example to fetch a short-lived token:
    - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - If you need persistent tokens, I can add Secret-backed tokens or kubeconfigs.
- Kubernetes API access from pods: With default-deny egress, in-cluster calls to the Kubernetes API are blocked unless explicitly allowed. If your workloads need this, tell me and I’ll add a precise egress allow rule (IPBlock/Service-based, depending on your cluster) following least privilege.
- If you want the full manifests as a single file for GitOps, I can output them or push a Kustomize/Helm structure.

- Print the full YAML manifests for version control?
- Add precise egress allowances to Kubernetes API or other system services your workloads require?
